title: Hardware Light Development, One Cycle, Four Phases
author: Uwe Mierisch
summary: Mierisch reconstructs the moment he became the most unpopular man in a truck engineering organisation by cancelling an entire prototype fleet, and uses it to explain why a technically correct transformation decision can still be the wrong one. His diagnosis of the resistance is the heart of the piece: hardware was never only a test object, it was a hygiene factor and a management instrument, the one milestone nobody could fudge because everyone could see who had failed to deliver. He then lays out the replacement, a single universal four-stroke cycle of definition, creation, validation and implementation that compresses the industry's four maturity levels into one pass, each phase gated by a hard definition of done. The precondition he calls the democratization of virtual prototypes is what makes it work, because a virtual fleet only enforces honesty if every project member can open it on their own machine rather than a handful of specialists. The confession at the end reframes the whole essay as a leadership lesson rather than a process one. He did not err in removing the fleet, he erred in removing it before the substitute existed, and he argues that people surrender a principle they have trusted for decades only when the replacement is demonstrably better.
points: Identifies the real function of a prototype fleet as schedule discipline and visible accountability, not engineering validation, which is why cancelling it felt like an attack.
Argues that prototype-driven development fails predictably rather than volatilely, since scarce vehicles plus one late engineer collapses every allocation plan every time.
Compresses four industry maturity levels into one cycle with hard definition-of-done gates, and bars new scope once validation begins.
Makes universal access to virtual prototypes the precondition rather than a nice-to-have, since a tool only specialists can open cannot replace a fleet everyone could walk up to.
Concludes that the sequencing error, not the decision, caused the revolt: the replacement has to be in place before the thing it replaces is taken away.
quotes: Hardware is concrete, you can touch it, and it is brutally honest.
I need the prototype fleet availability as a milestone that everyone simply has to take seriously, because it is unmistakably clear who has not delivered.
Let me be blunt. This is not unpredictable, it happens with absolute certainty, every single time. It is a property of this way of working.
Access to virtual prototypes has to be easy and available from day one for everyone working in the project.
Whoever cancels that fleet does not only cancel hardware. He cancels honesty and he cancels schedule discipline.
So my mistake was not the decision against the fleet. My mistake was the timing. I took the hardware away before the replacement was there.
This way of working demands something that is harder to procure than prototypes. It demands trust in something you cannot touch.
